Lemma

GeometryCirclesArea
What it shows: A curved shape made from four half-circles, next to a circle that sits on the upright line CF.
How to play: Drag the blue dot along the bottom line, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Press a button to jump to an end of the line.
Look for the math

Move the blue point and the curved shape changes size. Yet the number for its area below always matches the number for the circle on CF. Why must they agree?

Euclid's quiet identity

The article begins with Proposition II.10 of Euclid's Elements: if a straight line is bisected and then extended, then

(2m + n)² + n² = 2(m² + (m + n)²)

Put a = m + n and b = m, and it reads more clearly as

(a + b)² + (a − b)² = 2(a² + b²)

Here the bisected line is DE, so m = EO and the added piece is n = AD. Then a = OA, b = EO, and the identity says EA² + AD² = 2(EO² + OA²). The logic test checks both forms for all 12,321 pairs of whole numbers up to 110, and again for 2,000 large random pairs: the claim is true.

From squares to half-circles

Write L = AD = BE. Since E is as far from B as D is from A, DE = AB − 2L and CF = OA + EO = AB − L. The article's next step, AB² + DE² = 2(CF² + AD²), follows from the same identity. A semicircle on diameter d has area πd²/8, so multiplying by that common factor turns the squares into half-circles:

semi(AB) + semi(DE) = circle(CF) + semi(AD) + semi(BE)

Move the two small half-circles from the right to the left and the salinon is left on one side, the circle on CF on the other. This is Archimedes' Proposition 14, and the test confirms the identity for every one of the 111 lengths the applet can draw: π(AB − L)²/4 on both sides, exactly.

What the Java applet drew

The original applet started its dot 30% of the way from A to O, and the dot could only slide along that left half of the diameter: moving it to O made D and E meet at the centre, while moving it to A made the two small half-circles vanish. Its blue dot was picked up only when the mouse was within 5 pixels, and its drop test oddly demanded a point a little above the diameter although the dot always sat on it; both are presentation quirks and are not copied here. The applet's own "about" text called itself a demonstration of regular polygons, a leftover from another applet: the page's salinon description wins.

The live cut-the-knot page no longer embeds the Java applet; the archived page from 2012 does. The red fills here echo Roger Nelsen's proof without words, which the article says the applet was hinting at. The faint dashed spokes are the applet's own guide lines from the ends to C and from D, E to F.

The symmetric extreme

Press Symmetric (D = E): now DE is zero, CF equals OA, and the shape is the symmetric arbelos that the article mentions. The big half-circle has twice the area of the two small ones together, so the leftover equals the circle on the radius OA. At the other end, D = A, the salinon fills the whole big half-circle plus the inverted one, and the circle on CF is as large as it gets. The test checks both ends, and that the area falls strictly between them.

Try the Symmetric button, then drag the dot all the way back to A. Watch the two area numbers in the status line: they change together but never stop being equal.
